A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GPT-OSS-20B grid-world study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reordering and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original navigation experiments, instrumental and implicit goal tests, cognitive-map probing, and plan-decoding results in Sections 4–5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds top-k map evaluation, decoder-capacity comparisons, inverse recovery analysis, and activation-patching experiments.

M1.justification: v2 extends decoded-belief evaluation beyond single argmax locations to top-k candidate agent and goal locations. It also introduces one- and two-layer plan-decoder variants alongside the existing four-layer decoder, emphasizing the two-layer readout. The underlying agent and cognitive-map probing approach remain.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same grid navigation tasks, sizes, obstacle densities, key/door variants, and qualitative partial-observability tests. The new patching experiments use counterfactual positions within the existing 7×7 navigation setting; they introduce an intervention protocol rather than a new task or domain.

E2.justification: The plan-decoding comparison expands from four-layer readouts and random guessing in v1 Figure 9 to one-, two-, and four-layer readouts plus the same random baseline in v2 Figure 10. The optimal-policy and linear-versus-MLP comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds a controlled patching protocol using correctly solved 7×7 counterfactual pairs with disjoint optimal actions, four intervention sites, individual versus all-layer patches, both patching directions, and unchanged-action controls. It also adds top-k settings of 3, 5, and 10, decoder-depth comparisons, and an inverse recovery metric. Existing behavioural sampling and plan-decoder data splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Substantial new analyses examine whether location uncertainty explains actions, whether decoder capacity accounts for recovered plans, and whether intervening on representations changes behaviour. These include top-k sensitivity, inverse recovery, decoder-depth ablations, and controlled activation patching. Earlier layer, grid-size, distance, and trajectory-length analyses remain despite appendix relocation.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 9 adds error bars to ground-truth and top-1 decoded-policy accuracies previously reported as point estimates in Table 2. Their statistical meaning is unspecified. The existing trajectory repetition counts and Wilcoxon testing are retained; the patching execution counts do not establish additional seed-based repetitions.

E6.justification: New results include two-layer decoding accuracy of 66.49% post-reasoning versus 41.5% pre-reasoning at one step, top-k accuracy curves, and inverse recovery rates. Appendix F reports 0/456 action changes under single-layer patching and 144/144 stable control outcomes. These extend the evaluated configurations rather than establish a same-setting performance gain. Table 2 removes the average agent/goal Manhattan-distance columns.

T1.justification: Appendix E.4 introduces the inverse recovery definition: the proportion of actions suboptimal under the decoded map that are optimal under ground truth, reversing the conditioning used for recovery. The existing MDP/POMDP definitions, metric equations, and decoder mathematics are otherwise retained, without new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims: combining behavioural and representational evaluation, recovering coarse nonlinear spatial representations and plans, and observing a reasoning-related shift towards immediate action selection. The added analyses support and qualify this framing without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops the previously deferred multiple-map idea into an interpretation of planning under uncertain states. It also interprets non-monotonic decoder-capacity results as evidence against probe-generated planning and patching results as consistent with distributed state information. The conclusion now grounds its unresolved-causality limitation in attempted interventions and suggests alternative grid encodings.

D1.justification: v2 supplies two code-repository links and an interactive cognitive-map viewer, and newly discloses minority-class upsampling for probe training. This disclosure does not establish that the earlier training procedure changed. Appendix F additionally documents intervention sites and counterfactual filtering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Amin and Singh, Choi et al., Ivanitskiy et al., and Järviniemi et al. It qualifies behavioural goal identification under strong assumptions and connects intervention difficulties to distributed representation editing. The broader positioning remains; numerous bibliographic updates concern already cited works.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, related work, methods, interpretations, and conclusion are rewritten. v2 separates instrumental and implicit goal explanations, condenses Appendix A by removing unexecuted study plans, and reorganizes representational results and prompts into Appendices E–G.

P2.justification: Selected displays change: Figure 1 gains a multi-goal panel, a top-k accuracy figure is added, and the plan-decoding plot expands to six capacity/stage curves. Table 2 loses two columns, and the transformation plot uses a tighter vertical scale. Most existing plots and the two-column layout are retained.

improvement.justification: Decoder-capacity controls, uncertainty-sensitive evaluation, and controlled patching improve scrutiny of the representational claims; code links and class-balancing details improve reproducibility. The gains remain limited: causal links are unresolved, top-k scoring is more permissive, and successful all-layer patching is qualified by intervention site in Section 5.2 but described more broadly in Appendix F.
